claimed.line: Sarmast said sonar showed a walled hill and 2 to 3 km walls, 1.5 km down, about 80 km south-east of Cyprus.
claimed.evidence: Deep-water sonar scanning had indicated human-made structures on a submerged hill, including a 2-mile-long (3-kilometer-long) wall, a walled hill summit and deep trenches, he said.

found.line: Ships mapped this sea bed in 2003 and read the hills as salt, mud-volcano and fault features; a 2009 paper is reported to reject the walls.
found.evidence: complex surface deformation with small hills and linear depressions interpreted as due to the interaction between halokinetics, mud-diapirism and tectonics

needs_sea_level.when: within the last 11,000 years, as Sarmast dates the flood (between 10,000 and 30,000 BC in one report)
needs_sea_level.why: Sarmast's own model draws the 'island' at 1,650 m below today's sea, so the Mediterranean would have had to be dry in human times.
needs_sea_level.evidence: Model #2 shows the area at -1650 meters (almost one mile below today's water level), depicting the island as it would have appeared before the great flood that submerged Atlantis.

features.label: Sarmast's claimed 'Atlantis' site
features.what: Where Sarmast said his sonar found a walled hill and walls: about 80 km off the south-east coast of Cyprus, 1.5 km down.

position.detail: Only words: '50 miles (80 kilometers) off the southeast coast of Cyprus', 'between Cyprus and Syria', 1.5 km deep. No coordinates were published in any source I could open. Point is 80 km from Cape Greco (OSM node 34.9597 N, 34.0838 E) on a south-east bearing (135 degrees). Reuters of 13 Nov 2004 says 70 miles (about 113 km) 'off the eastern coast of Cyprus toward Syria'. GMRT depth at this point is 1,828 m, so the 1.5 km depth fits a point a little to the east or south-east of it.

features.evidence: led a team of explorers 50 miles (80 kilometers) off the southeast coast of Cyprus earlier this month. Deep-water sonar scanning had indicated human-made structures on a submerged hill
features.notes: The announced position is a description, not a fix. The Cyprus Mail (copy on Sarmast's site) says a Cyprus group gave a remote viewer 'Sarmast's co-ordinates', so Sarmast did have a position; I found it published nowhere. Keep the circle large.

features.label: French BLAC survey, Oct-Nov 2003
features.who: Benkhelil, Hubscher, Maillard, Tahchi and others (R/V Le Suroit)
features.what: A ship mapped about 20,000 square km of sea bed between Cyprus and Syria with a multibeam echo-sounder and shot seismic lines on 88 tracks.
features.result: The map shows the Larnaca-Latakia plateau, the Central domain at about 1,500 m, the Levantine basin at about 2,000 m and the Latakia Ridge; hills here are read as salt, mud-diapir and fault features.

position.detail: Outline of the coloured bathymetry in Fig. 2 (bathymetric map with E 34 deg to 36 deg and N 34 deg to 35 deg 30 min ticks). Control: the five tick marks on each edge, checked against Beirut, Tripoli, Tartus, Larnaca and Latakia, which fall within 3 to 9 pixels (about 1 to 4 km) of their true positions. The thin strip running south from the Latakia Ridge is left out.

features.evidence: the BLAC cruise aboard the R/V Le Suroît (October–November 2003) was designed to investigate an area of 20 000 km 2 between Cyprus and the margin of Syria, using a Simrad EM300 multibeam system
features.notes: Dates 29 Oct to 16 Nov 2003 (French text). The paper does not mention Sarmast. Cyprus Mail (20 Nov 2004) quotes a German physicist and two colleagues who say they 'surveyed the same area last year'; Hubscher is a BLAC co-author but no source I read names the speakers. The outline is the whole mapped area, so it includes ground far from the claimed site.

story.line: In 2003 Robert Sarmast's book 'Discovery of Atlantis' put the city on the sea bed south-east of Cyprus, a mile down.
In Oct and Nov 2003 a French research ship mapped 20,000 square km of this sea bed and shot seismic lines across it.
In Nov 2004 Sarmast sailed from Limassol for six days of sonar and announced a walled hill with walls 2 to 3 km long.
Within days, geologists said it was an old mud volcano and that they had surveyed the same area the year before.
The survey papers read these hills as salt folds, mud volcanoes and faults; a 2009 paper is reported to find no walls.
Drill cores 200 km west show deep-sea mud, and the Mediterranean last refilled 5.33 million years ago, long before people.

not_located.what: Sarmast's 'Acropolis Hill', its two walls (2 or 3 km) and the trenches, as he drew them
not_located.why: He published only 3D models, animations and one image, none with a latitude and longitude or a scale bar that I could open; the announced position is a verbal description.

not_located.what: The ship track and sonar box of the November 2004 expedition (vessel Flying Enterprise, six days)
not_located.why: No positions printed in the news reports or on the expedition pages I read.

not_located.what: The 'Atlantis capsule' put on the sea bed on 30 April 2004 at the 'Atlantis site'
not_located.why: The Aquatec page gives a depth (1,600 m) but no coordinates.

not_located.what: Seismic lines and multibeam tracks of Hubscher and others' 2009 paper (the 2003 Le Suroit BLAC data and, as one search result put it, a 2004 R/V Pelagia cruise called SAGA)
not_located.why: The paper is behind a paywall and its map figures could not be read; only the open BLAC paper (2005) was digitised.

not_located.what: The History Channel seismic profile said to show the walls as natural landforms
not_located.why: Only seen as a one-line description on Wikipedia; no position.

handoffs.what: Add the 2003 BLAC cruise (R/V Le Suroit, 29 Oct to 16 Nov 2003, Simrad EM300, 88 profiles) as a search; Benkhelil and others 2005 is open and gives dates and area.

Ifremer's cruise page for BLAC and its navigation file, or the EMODnet/SISMER survey outline (a SISMER survey 38467 is noted in site-data.json at nearby points), would replace my hand-digitised outline.
ODP Leg 160 Sites 965 to 968 on the Eratosthenes Seamount are given here as context only; the seamount has its own Atlantis claims.

not_verified: The text of Hubscher and others 2009 (Tectonophysics 470, 173-182): ScienceDirect and ResearchGate blocked scripts and Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar hold no abstract. What it says about the Atlantis claim comes only from Wikipedia ('demonstrated that the features which Sarmast interprets to be Atlantis consist only of a natural compressional fold caused by local salt tectonics and a slide scar'). I could not tell whether the paper itself mentions Sarmast.

That the German physicist quoted by the Cyprus Mail is Hubscher: the article does not name him. The National Center for Public Policy Research page names Huebscher, but it is an opinion source and I did not fetch it.
A research cruise called SAGA on R/V Pelagia in 2004 and its 600 m streamer: stated in a search-tool summary of the ScienceDirect page that I could not open myself.

The 2006 follow-up: Sarmast's own updates page (Feb to May 2006) says a second expedition 'may also happen this spring/summer season depending on the availability of funds'; I found no record that it took place.
The original BBC and CNN pages: the BBC text is read from the copy on Sarmast's own site (Wayback Machine, Dec 2004), not from bbc.co.uk.

John Hall and others on Levant bathymetry, Maillard and others 2011 on the Latakia Ridge, EMODnet survey outlines for the Cyprus Basin, and replies by Michael Hall or other Cypriot geologists: not fetched or not found.
GMRT and the EMODnet tiles were not checked for survey outlines; the depth figure is one GMRT point query.
